analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee — it held hearings in March 2001 but never approved it, no other senator signed on, and the Senate never voted.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently erased the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for everyone dying or giving gifts after December 31, 2000 [S2] [S3]. The estate tax at the time applied only to the largest estates — those above the exemption threshold — so the people who would keep the most money are heirs to the wealthiest families [S2]. The government would lose the revenue those taxes bring in, which means other taxpayers or federal programs would eventually absorb the difference.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to large estates — the families whose inheritances were big enough to owe the tax — would keep everything instead of paying estate and generation-skipping taxes on it. Owners of family farms and businesses large enough to be taxable would no longer face a bill at death, and wealthy families could give large gifts tax-free [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Permanently repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2000, so taxable estates would owe nothing and heirs would inherit the full amount

Because only estates above the exemption threshold owed the tax, the benefit is concentrated: the largest family fortunes, farms, and businesses get the full exemption while most families, whose estates were below the threshold, were unaffected either way

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury loses all estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax revenue, and that money has to come from somewhere — other taxes, more borrowing, or smaller federal spending — so ordinary taxpayers and the programs funded by general revenue bear the cost [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The repeal is permanent and unconditional: it removes a source of federal revenue with no replacement, shifting the burden onto other taxpayers, borrowing, or spending cuts

The benefits are highly concentrated. Only estates above the exemption threshold owed the tax at all, so the money goes to a small number of the wealthiest families while most households see no benefit — only the shared cost of the lost revenue

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a narrow slice of the wealthiest families, while the cost — a permanent loss of federal revenue — is spread across every taxpayer. There is no offset or phase-in to soften the revenue hit. As drafted, the bill's benefits and costs do not come close to balancing for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee — which held one round of hearings but never approved it — and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wayne Allard introduced the bill on January 22, 2001, the day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee
No senator joined as a cosponsor at any point
The Finance Committee held hearings on March 15, 2001, but never reported the bill out of committee, so the full Senate never considered it
The bill expired at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003, without ever reaching a floor vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury kept the estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax revenue, and heirs to large estates did not get the repeal. Ordinary taxpayers were spared picking up the cost of a tax cut aimed at the largest fortunes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The treasury, which kept estate tax revenue

for.name: Sen. Wayne Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; no other senator cosponsored it

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on March 15, 2001, but never reported the bill to the full Senate, keeping it from any floor vote

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote was ever taken and no senator besides Allard signed on, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: Only estates above the exemption threshold owed the tax, so repeal would transfer its entire value to heirs of the largest fortunes. The gain for those families is the revenue the rest of taxpayers would have to replace.

industries.industry: Estate planning and estate-tax life insurance services
industries.note: A standing estate tax creates steady demand for lawyers and advisors who plan around it and for insurance sold to cover the bill. Repeal would shrink that business, though the effect on ordinary people is small either way.
